title: Population Ecology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L Botany/Plant Science Population Ecology curriculum: population characteristics (density, natality, mortality), population growth models (exponential and logistic), carrying capacity, survivorship curves, life tables, population regulation (density-dependent/independent factors), dispersion patterns, intraspecific and interspecific competition, r- and K-selection, and metapopulation concepts.

questions.question: In ecology, a population is best defined as:
options: All organisms of different species living in an area
A group of individuals of the same species living in a defined geographic area at a given time, capable of interbreeding
A single organism and its immediate offspring only
All the biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem
questions.correct_answer: A group of individuals of the same species living in a defined geographic area at a given time, capable of interbreeding
questions.explanation: A population is defined at the species level -- individuals of one species occupying a given area and time, sharing a common gene pool.

questions.question: Population density refers to:
options: The total number of species in a community
The number of individuals per unit area or volume
The rate of population growth
The proportion of males to females
questions.correct_answer: The number of individuals per unit area or volume
questions.explanation: Density is a basic population attribute expressing abundance relative to space, e.g. number of trees per hectare.

questions.question: Natality in population ecology refers to:
options: The death rate of a population
The birth rate; production of new individuals
Movement of individuals into a population
Movement of individuals out of a population
questions.correct_answer: The birth rate; production of new individuals
questions.explanation: Natality is the rate of production of new individuals through reproduction, one of the four key processes (with mortality, immigration, emigration) that change population size.

questions.question: Which combination of processes determines the rate of change of population size?
options: Natality and mortality only
Natality, mortality, immigration and emigration
Photosynthesis and respiration
Predation and parasitism only
questions.correct_answer: Natality, mortality, immigration and emigration
questions.explanation: Population size changes according to: births + immigrants - deaths - emigrants; all four processes must be considered for a complete population growth model.

questions.question: The exponential growth model (dN/dt = rN) describes population growth under which condition?
options: Unlimited resources with no environmental resistance
Resources that are limiting and cause density-dependent regulation
A population at carrying capacity
A population experiencing only emigration
questions.correct_answer: Unlimited resources with no environmental resistance
questions.explanation: Exponential (J-shaped) growth assumes an idealised environment with unlimited resources, so growth rate is proportional only to population size (r), producing continuously accelerating growth.

questions.question: In the logistic growth equation dN/dt = rN(1 - N/K), the term (1 - N/K) represents:
options: The intrinsic rate of increase
Environmental resistance that slows growth as population approaches carrying capacity
The mortality rate alone
The immigration rate
questions.correct_answer: Environmental resistance that slows growth as population approaches carrying capacity
questions.explanation: As N approaches K, the term (1 - N/K) approaches zero, progressively reducing the realised growth rate and producing the characteristic S-shaped (sigmoid) logistic curve.

questions.question: Carrying capacity (K) of an environment is defined as:
options: The maximum population size that an environment can sustain indefinitely given available resources
The minimum viable population size
The intrinsic rate of natural increase
The rate of resource renewal
questions.correct_answer: The maximum population size that an environment can sustain indefinitely given available resources
questions.explanation: K represents the upper asymptote of the logistic growth curve, set by the limits of resources such as food, space and nutrients in a given environment.

questions.question: A population growth curve that rises steeply then levels off abruptly at carrying capacity, producing a J-shape followed by a crash, is typical of:
options: Smooth logistic growth
Population overshoot and crash (boom-and-bust) dynamics
Zero population growth from the start
Constant exponential decline
questions.correct_answer: Population overshoot and crash (boom-and-bust) dynamics
questions.explanation: When growth is rapid and density-dependent feedback is delayed, populations can overshoot K and then crash due to resource depletion, rather than smoothly approaching K.

questions.question: A Type I survivorship curve, as in humans and many large mammals, is characterised by:
options: High mortality in early life with few survivors reaching old age
Constant mortality rate throughout life
Low mortality until late in life, with most individuals surviving to old age
Mortality that decreases with age from birth
questions.correct_answer: Low mortality until late in life, with most individuals surviving to old age
questions.explanation: Type I curves show high survivorship through most of the lifespan with mortality concentrated in old age, typical of species with parental care and few offspring.

questions.question: A Type III survivorship curve, typical of many plants and organisms producing numerous offspring with little parental care, shows:
options: Constant mortality rate at all ages
Very high mortality early in life (e.g. seeds/seedlings) with few survivors reaching maturity
Low mortality throughout life
High mortality only in old age
questions.correct_answer: Very high mortality early in life (e.g. seeds/seedlings) with few survivors reaching maturity
questions.explanation: Type III curves reflect strategies producing many offspring (e.g. seeds, spores) of which very few survive early stages, but those that do survive have relatively low subsequent mortality.

questions.question: A life table is a tool used in population ecology to:
options: Summarise age-specific survivorship and fecundity of a cohort or population
List the taxonomic classification of species
Record the geographic distribution of a species
Measure soil nutrient content
questions.correct_answer: Summarise age-specific survivorship and fecundity of a cohort or population
questions.explanation: Life tables track a cohort through age classes, recording number surviving, mortality rate and reproductive output at each age, used to compute survivorship curves and net reproductive rate.

questions.question: The net reproductive rate (R0) calculated from a life table represents:
options: The average number of offspring produced per individual per generation
The instantaneous rate of population growth
The carrying capacity of the environment
The death rate of the population
questions.correct_answer: The average number of offspring produced per individual per generation
questions.explanation: R0 is the sum of age-specific survivorship multiplied by fecundity across all ages, giving the mean number of offspring an individual leaves in the next generation; R0 > 1 indicates a growing population.

questions.question: Density-dependent factors regulating population size (e.g. competition, disease, predation) are characterised by:
options: Their effect intensifying as population density increases
Acting with equal intensity regardless of population size
Only affecting small populations
Being purely abiotic in nature
questions.correct_answer: Their effect intensifying as population density increases
questions.explanation: Density-dependent factors have a proportionally greater regulatory effect (e.g. more disease transmission, more competition) as population density rises, tending to stabilise populations near K.

questions.question: Which of the following is typically a density-independent factor affecting population size?
options: Intraspecific competition for food
A sudden severe frost or fire
Predation pressure
Disease transmission rate
questions.correct_answer: A sudden severe frost or fire
questions.explanation: Density-independent factors such as extreme weather events, fire or flooding affect a fixed proportion of a population regardless of its density, unlike competition, predation or disease.

questions.question: Intraspecific competition refers to competition:
options: Between individuals of different species
Between individuals of the same species for the same limited resources
Between predator and prey species
Between a parasite and its host
questions.correct_answer: Between individuals of the same species for the same limited resources
questions.explanation: Intraspecific competition occurs among members of a single species competing for resources such as light, water, nutrients or space, and is a key density-dependent regulator.

questions.question: Interspecific competition occurs when:
options: Two or more different species compete for the same limited resource
Individuals of the same species cooperate
A species competes only with itself
One species preys directly on another
questions.correct_answer: Two or more different species compete for the same limited resource
questions.explanation: Interspecific competition is competition between individuals of different species for shared limiting resources, which can lead to competitive exclusion or resource partitioning.

questions.question: The competitive exclusion principle (Gause's principle) states that:
options: Two species with identical ecological niches cannot coexist indefinitely in the same habitat
All competing species eventually cooperate
Competition always benefits both species
Species with different niches always compete strongly
questions.correct_answer: Two species with identical ecological niches cannot coexist indefinitely in the same habitat
questions.explanation: Gause's competitive exclusion principle holds that complete competitors for identical resources cannot stably coexist; one will outcompete and displace the other, unless niche differentiation occurs.

questions.question: Species that reduce competition by using different resources or habitats within an area are showing:
options: Resource/niche partitioning
Competitive exclusion
Predation
Mutualism
questions.correct_answer: Resource/niche partitioning
questions.explanation: Niche/resource partitioning allows ecologically similar species to coexist by dividing up resources along axes such as space, time, or food type, reducing direct competition.

questions.question: In population dispersion patterns, a 'clumped' (aggregated) distribution most commonly results from:
options: Uniform resource availability and strong territoriality
Patchy resource distribution or social/reproductive behaviour such as seed dispersal near the parent plant
Strong negative interactions between individuals spacing them evenly
Completely random settlement independent of resources
questions.correct_answer: Patchy resource distribution or social/reproductive behaviour such as seed dispersal near the parent plant
questions.explanation: Clumped distribution, the commonest pattern in nature, arises when resources are patchily distributed or when reproduction (e.g. seeds falling near the parent) and social behaviour concentrate individuals together.

questions.question: A uniform (regular) dispersion pattern in a plant population is most likely to result from:
options: Strong intraspecific competition for resources such as light and water, e.g. through allelopathy or root competition
Clustering of seeds by wind in one spot
Random dispersal with no interactions
Absence of any competition
questions.correct_answer: Strong intraspecific competition for resources such as light and water, e.g. through allelopathy or root competition
questions.explanation: Uniform spacing arises when strong negative interactions (competition, allelopathy, territoriality) cause individuals to be evenly spaced, minimising resource overlap.

questions.question: r-selected species are typically characterised by:
options: Large body size, long lifespan, few offspring with high parental investment
Small body size, short lifespan, rapid reproduction, many offspring with little parental care
Stable populations always at carrying capacity
Strong competitive ability under crowded conditions
questions.correct_answer: Small body size, short lifespan, rapid reproduction, many offspring with little parental care
questions.explanation: r-selected species are adapted to exploit unstable or unpredictable environments by maximising intrinsic growth rate (r) through rapid reproduction and high offspring number, e.g. many weeds and annual plants.

questions.question: K-selected species are typically adapted to:
options: Unpredictable, disturbed habitats requiring rapid colonisation
Stable environments near carrying capacity, favouring competitive ability, larger size and fewer, well-provisioned offspring
Producing thousands of offspring with no parental investment
Extremely short generation times
questions.correct_answer: Stable environments near carrying capacity, favouring competitive ability, larger size and fewer, well-provisioned offspring
questions.explanation: K-selected species thrive in stable, resource-limited environments where competitive ability matters more than rapid reproduction, e.g. many long-lived forest trees.

questions.question: Which of the following plant life-history traits is most typical of an r-strategist pioneer/weed species?
options: Long-lived perennial with slow growth and shade tolerance
Short-lived annual, rapid growth, abundant small seeds, good disperser
Very slow seed production and low dispersal ability
Requiring stable, undisturbed habitat
questions.correct_answer: Short-lived annual, rapid growth, abundant small seeds, good disperser
questions.explanation: Pioneer/weedy species exploit disturbed habitats by growing and reproducing quickly, producing many easily dispersed seeds, consistent with r-selection.

questions.question: A metapopulation is best described as:
options: A single, continuous, panmictic population
A set of spatially separated local populations of the same species that interact through occasional dispersal/migration
A community of different species
The total global population of a species with no substructure
questions.correct_answer: A set of spatially separated local populations of the same species that interact through occasional dispersal/migration
questions.explanation: Metapopulation theory (Levins) describes a 'population of populations' linked by migration among habitat patches, with local extinctions and recolonisations shaping regional persistence.

questions.question: In metapopulation dynamics, a local population that has gone extinct in a habitat patch can be re-established through:
options: Colonisation from a nearby occupied patch
Spontaneous generation
Increased predation
Habitat fragmentation alone
questions.correct_answer: Colonisation from a nearby occupied patch
questions.explanation: Recolonisation of empty but suitable patches by dispersers from occupied patches is central to metapopulation persistence despite local extinctions.

questions.question: The intrinsic rate of natural increase (r) of a population is highest when:
options: Birth rate greatly exceeds death rate under optimal, unlimited conditions
Birth rate equals death rate
Death rate exceeds birth rate
The population is at carrying capacity
questions.correct_answer: Birth rate greatly exceeds death rate under optimal, unlimited conditions
questions.explanation: r (= b - d, birth rate minus death rate) is maximal (rmax, the biotic potential) under ideal conditions with abundant resources and no environmental resistance.

questions.question: Environmental resistance refers to:
options: The sum of factors (e.g. limited food, predation, disease, competition) that limit population growth
The genetic resistance of a species to pesticides
The intrinsic growth rate of a population
The tendency of soil to resist erosion
questions.correct_answer: The sum of factors (e.g. limited food, predation, disease, competition) that limit population growth
questions.explanation: Environmental resistance encompasses all limiting factors that prevent a population from achieving its full biotic potential, keeping actual growth below the exponential maximum.

questions.question: Self-thinning in dense even-aged plant populations, described by the '-3/2 power law', refers to:
options: A predictable decline in the number of surviving individuals as average plant size (biomass) increases with age due to density-dependent mortality
Random death unrelated to density
An increase in plant number as biomass increases
A phenomenon restricted to animal populations
questions.correct_answer: A predictable decline in the number of surviving individuals as average plant size (biomass) increases with age due to density-dependent mortality
questions.explanation: As plants in a dense cohort grow, competition for light, water and nutrients causes progressive mortality of smaller individuals, following a characteristic self-thinning trajectory relating log mean plant weight to log density.

questions.question: Allee effects in population ecology describe a situation where:
options: Population growth rate decreases at low population density (positive density dependence)
Population growth rate always increases indefinitely
Population size has no effect on individual fitness
Only large populations experience reduced fitness
questions.correct_answer: Population growth rate decreases at low population density (positive density dependence)
questions.explanation: The Allee effect describes reduced individual fitness (e.g. via difficulty finding mates or reduced group protection) at low population densities, contrary to standard density-dependent regulation, and is important in conservation of small populations.

questions.question: Age structure (age distribution) of a population, showing the proportion of individuals in pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive classes, is useful for:
options: Predicting future population growth trends
Determining the soil type of the habitat
Measuring photosynthetic rate
Classifying plant taxonomy
questions.correct_answer: Predicting future population growth trends
questions.explanation: A population with a high proportion of pre-reproductive individuals (expanding age pyramid) predicts future growth, while a large post-reproductive class suggests decline, making age structure a key demographic tool.

questions.question: In plant population studies, a 'seed bank' refers to:
options: A financial institution funding agricultural research
The reservoir of viable, ungerminated seeds present in the soil at a given site
A collection of herbarium specimens
The total leaf biomass of a population
questions.correct_answer: The reservoir of viable, ungerminated seeds present in the soil at a given site
questions.explanation: The soil seed bank represents dormant, viable seeds accumulated over time, buffering plant populations against disturbance and enabling regeneration after events like fire or clearing.

questions.question: Which sampling method is commonly used to estimate plant population density in the field using randomly placed sample units?
options: Mark-recapture method
Quadrat sampling
Pitfall trapping
Electrofishing
questions.correct_answer: Quadrat sampling
questions.explanation: Quadrats -- fixed-area sample plots placed randomly or systematically -- are the standard method for estimating plant density, frequency and cover, unlike mark-recapture which is used for mobile animals.
